paragraphs.text: Lesson 24, language learning.
Pat is getting married and he's determined to learn his future wife's native language.
He talks with John about his difficulties.
Listen and answer the 10 comprehension questions.
How can I learn to speak Russian when I don't even understand how to read it?
And the wedding is just six months away.
There's no way, John.
There's just no way I can learn to speak Russian before then.
You're the one who's marrying a Russian bride, but hey, chill out, Pat.
The important thing is that you learn the basics.
No one can really learn a language fluently in six months, not that I know of at least.
I know, but Veronica and I promised each other that we would learn each other's language
before our wedding.
English isn't exactly rocket science, but Russian sure seems like it.
Hey, don't knock the English language.
How do you know Veronica isn't having the same way as you are?
I remember when I took classes to learn French.
I wanted to learn the romantic language to sweep Tory off her feet.
Yeah, I remember.
You're pretty fluent now, aren't you?
Yeah, but not at first, Pat.
We're from Georgia.
When I first started to learn French, I sounded like a drunken French hillbilly.
Not only did I have to learn the ins and outs of the language, I had to get the hang of the
accent.
Tory couldn't stop laughing the first time I spoke French to her.
You seem to be doing okay now, though.
And all it took was five years of forcing my mouth to get rid of my southern drawl and
try to sound like a French aristocrat.
I don't have five years.
And now that you mention it, I didn't even think about my accent.
Oh, man, I'm going to sound like a Russian hillbilly.
No, you won't.
You were raised in the capital.
My point is that learning a new language takes time.
I bet you ten bucks Veronica will not be speaking fluent English by the time of your wedding.
And she's got a thick Russian accent.
Maybe so, John, but at least she already speaks decent English.
I can't even say hello in Russian yet.
I can just see us saying our vows.
I'm supposed to say mine in Russian and Veronica is supposed to say hers in English.
What if I mess up and swear my eternal love to her left shoe or something?
You will not now stop it.
Listen to me.
You're a pretty smart fella.
The only mistake you're making is allowing a language to intimidate you.
I admit the Russian language isn't a piece of cake, but surely you can make a dent in it.
I know, I know.
Maybe I'm just worried about the wedding.
You know, being a married man and all.
I love Veronica, but the thought of a lifelong commitment.
You'll be just fine.
And if you do love Veronica, which you just admitted, then you'll learn the Russian language
for her sake.
Or at least so you can argue with your mother and all.
Ugh, don't remind me.
It's true though.
There's nothing in the world that I wouldn't do for Veronica.
So man up and start studying.
Alright, here.
Help quiz me on these flashcards so I don't make a fool of myself.
Here's an explanation of the vocabulary from the dialogue between Pat and John.
John says, hey, chill out, Pat.
Chill out is an informal way to tell somebody to relax.
Pat says that English isn't exactly rocket science.
He's saying that in his opinion, English isn't extremely difficult.
And John replies, hey, don't knock the English language.
Don't knock means don't make fun of or don't insult the English language.
John also learned another language to try to sweep Tori off her feet.
To sweep her off her feet means to make her fall in love with me very quickly.
John has an accent from the southern part of the United States.
And when he first started to learn French, he sounded like a drunken French hillbilly.
The adjective drunken describes when you have consumed too much alcohol.
We can also say a person is drunk.
This is the more common way to say it.
And a hillbilly is someone from the countryside, from a less developed part of the country.
John says, not only did I have to learn the ins and outs of the language, I had to get the
hang of the accent.
The ins and outs are all the tiny details.
And get the hang of means to learn something by practicing.
Pat says that John's French is now pretty good, and John says it took five years of forcing
his mouth to get rid of his southern draw.
Get rid of means to remove.
And the expression southern draw refers to the accent from the southern part of the United
States.
It's often called a draw, a slow way of speaking that prolongs the words.
John tried to sound like a French aristocrat.
An aristocrat is a member of the ruling class or nobility.
But Pat doesn't have five years to learn.
He only has a few months.
John reassures him by saying, I bet you ten bucks Veronica will not be speaking fluent English
by the time of your wedding.
I bet you ten bucks is a way of saying I'm completely sure that.
And, as John points out, Veronica has a thick Russian accent.
If someone has a thick accent, it means they have a strong accent, and it's maybe a little
bit difficult to understand them.
Pat and Veronica are planning to say their vows in each other's languages.
Vows are the very strong promises made between the two people getting married.
Pat is worried about messing up.
To mess up means to make a mistake.
He says, what if I mess up and swear my eternal love to her left shoe?
The verb swear in this context means to promise strongly.
John tells Pat to listen to him, saying, you're a pretty smart fella.
The word fella is an informal way to say fellow.
A fellow is a guy or a man.
John says the only mistake Pat is making is allowing a new language to intimidate him.
If something intimidates you, it makes you feel scared and threatened.
John admits that the Russian language isn't a piece of cake.
This expression means it isn't easy.
However, surely Pat can make a dent in it.
To make a dent in something means to make at least a small amount of progress in a big task.
Pat expresses some other worries about the commitment to marriage.
And John says, if you love Veronica, you'll learn the Russian language for her sake.
For her sake means for her benefit or because of her.
Or, John points out, Pat could learn the language so he could argue with his mother-in-law.
Your mother-in-law is the mother of your husband or wife.
And the father of your husband or wife is your father-in-law.
Your husband or wife's siblings are your brothers-in-law and sisters-in-law.
Pat replies, ugh, don't remind me.
Don't remind me means I don't want to think about that.
So he doesn't want to think about potential arguments with his future wife's mother.
But he admits that he would do anything in the world for Veronica.
So John says, man up and start studying.
The phrasal verb, man up, means be courageous, take initiative.
This phrasal verb is typically only used among men when one man is talking to another and encouraging him to be brave, to be a man.
So Pat finally asks John to help quiz him on some flashcards so that he doesn't make a fool of himself.
To make a fool of yourself means to do something that makes you appear silly or stupid.
That's all the vocabulary from today's conversation.
Go ahead and try the vocabulary quiz to put these expressions into practice and the speaking task to get some feedback on your spoken English.
